Andre Breton. André Breton (1896-1966) was a French poet, essayist, and artist who founded Surrealism in 1924, shaping one of the twentieth century's most influential artistic movements. Through manifestos, theoretical writings, and tireless curation of artists, Breton established Surrealism as a philosophy of liberation-using psychoanalytic concepts of the unconscious, dream logic, and creative automatism to challenge rational, bourgeois culture. Though his authoritarian control over Surrealism generated tension and defection, Breton's vision fundamentally altered how artists understood creativity, meaning, and the power of the irrational. Published the Surrealist Manifesto (1924), declaring the movement's allegiance to the unconscious, dreams, and the liberation of the imagination from rational constraint. In addition, began his career with Dada after World War I, but became disillusioned with Dada's pure negation; Surrealism retained Dada's revolt but sought to build something affirmative. Similarly, grounded Surrealism in Sigmund Freud's theories of the unconscious and dream analysis, treating art-making as a means to access hidden psychological depths. Another important aspect is that championed automatism-the practice of spontaneous, unplanned creation (automatic drawing, automatic writing)-as a path to bypass conscious control and rational judgment. It's also worth knowing that organized surrealist exhibitions, maintained a famous Paris salon, and published the journal La Révolution Surréaliste, exerting considerable curatorial and editorial authority. Also worth noting is that collaborated intensely with artists including Max Ernst, Salvador Dalí, and many others; his endorsements and rejections significantly shaped careers. In addition, eventually expelled or rejected several major surrealists, including Dalí, over philosophical differences or perceived betrayals; these rifts fractured the movement's unity. Most notably, remained committed to Surrealism through World War II and beyond, despite the movement's fragmentation and the rise of competing avant-gardes. centered context from which Surrealism radiated internationally.
